quotes.text: with a few more years under his belt he became a better communicator through his vocals. True, in the 70s he never let rip like the rampaging rocker he was in the late 50s, back when he was a young man whose voice shook the world – but I think Elvis in the late 60s/early 70s was more skilled and nuanced vocally than he was when he started out, was better at putting warmth and pain and longing into his vocals

for a brief couple of years he was hungry again, and this set captures that moment in time with an unadorned, naked portrait of a vocalist who was truly peerless. Despite my initial skepticism, From Elvis in Nashville really needed to be released so the world could better hear those amazing vocals.
The horns and strings on That's the Way It Is would never have worked had they not been laid over such brilliant basic instrumental tracks.

Elvis was an original. He didn't fit the mold of a singer at that time. He synthesized the feel of gospel and blues with a rockabilly kick and a love of Hank Snow, so you couldn't peg him to any of the existing genres.

What made him seem even more alien was that he had to move while singing, something that would later drive the recording engineers at RCA up a wall because the bastard kept moving off the spot they had marked for him. Finally, they gave in, surrounded him with mikes and let Elvis be Elvis.

Sam Phillips of Sun considered him little more than a possible ballad singer until, at the end of an unfruitful recording session, Elvis and his boys started playing around with "That's All Right" and Sam heard exactly what he'd been looking for: a white guy who captured the sound of the black guys.
Once Colonel Parker arrived on the scene, the songs started to get cute, the delivery more polished and that marvelous kinetic energy faded into memory.

"Blue Suede Shoes" is a hell of an opener, in large part because of the shock of the stop-time opening where Elvis belts it out with maximum intensity. While I love Carl Perkins' version, and bemoan the fact that he rarely gets credit for his contributions to rock, Elvis' version is so much sexier.
The best rock 'n' roll has the curious effect of lifting our spirits and fanning our flames, and Elvis was one of the first to work that kind of magic.

I think one aspect of Elvis' music that made him a bit more palatable to the mass audience than Little Richard or Chuck Berry had nothing to do with race, but with his willingness to sing tender ballads.

Maybe on stage – he was 100% responsible for his sound on stage, he put the band together, he added the Sweet Inspirations and the Imperials and the orchestra and Kathy Westmoreland the Warbling Banshee Desecrator of Decent Songs, he chose the material and conceptualized the arrangements and got exactly the sound he wanted onstage and all of that – to the extent a rock concert is art, Elvis was an artist, I will grant you that.

He never treated an album as an art form – as a matter of fact, he never really seemed to put much thought into them at all. When he was firing on all cylinders he could put a lot of thought into individual songs, although more frequently he was just interested in seeing how many songs he could knock out in one session so RCA would quit bugging him for more material.

Elvis seemed to think once the tape stopped rolling, his job was done. Once he walked out of the studio door he seemed content to let Felton Jarvis, his producer for much of his career, handle things after that. So on an album you get Elvis' performances, but not really his vision for an album.

Elvis never did anything close to that, other than crappy soundtracks that helped tell the story of crappy movies, and those aren't art. So, no, I don't really consider Elvis an artist as far as his albums are concerned, however fantastic many of them are as a collection of songs. Elvis never tried to make an album an artistic statement – it was more like "here, have a few songs".
